extraction.name: Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD)
extraction.description: A reading comprehension dataset consisting of 100,000+ questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles, where the answer to each question is a segment of text from the corresponding reading passage.
extraction.creator: Pranav Rajpurkar and Jian Zhang and Konstantin Lopyrev and Percy Liang
extraction.citeAs: Pranav Rajpurkar and Jian Zhang and Konstantin Lopyrev and Percy Liang. SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text. arXiv:1606.05250v3 [cs.CL], 2016.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected in three stages: curating passages, crowdsourcing question-answer pairs on those passages, and obtaining additional answers. The authors used Project Nayuki's Wikipedia internal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia, sampled 536 articles uniformly at random, extracted individual paragraphs, stripped away images, figures, and tables, and discarded paragraphs shorter than 500 characters. Crowdworkers then asked and answered up to 5 questions per paragraph, entering questions in a text field and highlighting answer spans in the paragraph. Additional answers were later collected for each question in the development and test sets.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Over the development and test sets, 2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at least one of the additional crowdworkers.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: English Wikipedia articles. The authors used Project Nayuki's Wikipedia internal PageRanks to obtain the top 10000 articles of English Wikipedia, sampled 536 articles, and extracted 23,215 paragraphs after stripping away images, figures, and tables and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: From sampled Wikipedia articles, the authors extracted individual paragraphs, stripped away images, figures, and tables, discarded paragraphs shorter than 500 characters, and randomly partitioned the articles into training set (80%), development set (10%), and test set (10%).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Paragraphs were extracted from Wikipedia articles after removing images, figures, and tables and filtering out paragraphs shorter than 500 characters. For modeling, candidate answer spans were restricted to constituents in constituency parses generated by Stanford CoreNLP; when a correct answer was not a constituent during training, the shortest constituent containing the correct answer was used as the target.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers created question-answer pairs for each paragraph by asking and answering up to 5 questions on the paragraph content. Questions were entered in a text field and answers were highlighted in the paragraph. Tasks included a sample paragraph and examples of good and bad questions and answers with explanations. Workers were encouraged to ask questions in their own words without copying phrases from the paragraph. For development and test sets, at least 2 additional answers were collected per question by showing workers the questions and paragraphs and asking them to select the shortest span answering the question, or submit the question without marking an answer if it was not answerable by a span.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Daemo platform with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: To assess human performance and make evaluation more robust, each question in the development and test sets had at least three answers. Human performance was measured by treating the second answer as the human prediction and the other answers as ground truth. Human F1 of 86.8% was based on interannotator agreement. Mismatch occurred mostly due to inclusion or exclusion of non-essential phrases rather than fundamental disagreements. Over the development and test sets, 2.6% of questions were marked unanswerable by at least one additional crowdworker.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 answers per question in the development and test sets; initially 1 question-answer annotation per created question, with up to 5 questions authored per paragraph.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowdworkers were required to have a 97% HIT acceptance rate, a minimum of 1000 HITs, and be located in the United States or Canada.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper identifies the dataset as Stanford Question Answering Dataset v1.0 and notes later results on SQuAD v1.1, but does not describe an updating timeframe, maintainers, or deprecation policies.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to encourage exploration of more expressive models for reading comprehension and natural language understanding, with the authors expecting efforts on the dataset to result in significant advances in reading comprehension.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that crowdworkers were located in the United States or Canada and were encouraged to ask questions in their own words. It also reports that 2.6% of questions in development and test were marked unanswerable by at least one additional crowdworker, and that some sampled examples were ambiguous or did not have a unique answer.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset constrains answers to spans from the passage, making questions more constrained than more interpretative questions in advanced standardized tests. In manual analysis, some examples were ambiguous or did not have a unique answer. For modeling, only 77.3% of correct answers in the development set were constituents, placing an effective ceiling on methods restricted to constituent spans.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is presented as a reading comprehension and machine question answering benchmark. It is partitioned into training, development, and test sets and is used for training and evaluating machine comprehension models.
